description: created with a blind musician's perspective, bringing Earth data to everyone through sound
summary: What does a changing planet sound like? Earth Voices & Resonance transforms three NASA Earth science records—global temperature (1880–2025), nighttime lights (2012–2023), and lightning observations (2017–2023)—into an interactive listening experience. Warmer years produce higher notes, changing nighttime brightness creates rising or falling pitches, and lightning patterns reveal seasonal rhythms. Users can customize instruments, pitch ranges, and playback speed while exploring synchronized charts and data tables. Co-created by a legally blind student, the project draws on firsthand experience with NVDA and Microsoft Magnifier to guide its accessibility-focused design. Our Earth Information Jukebox invites blind, low-vision, and sighted learners to investigate the same planetary changes through sound, sight, and text—making accessibility part of scientific discovery.
details:
1. What does your project do, and how does it work?

Earthtone lets people hear a changing planet. Co-created by a legally blind student, it turns NASA information about global temperature, nighttime lights, and lightning into sound.

Each note represents a point in time, with higher values mapped to higher pitches. Users can explore the timeline, follow synchronized charts and measurements, and customize instruments, musical scales, pitch ranges, speed, and volume.

Temperature measurements come from NASA GISTEMP. Nighttime lights and lightning use relative indicators extracted from NASA visualization videos.

2. What benefits does it have?

Earthtone makes visual information available through sound while keeping charts and numerical values available for reference. Users can listen to an entire record or explore individual points at their own pace.

Keyboard controls, screen-reader labels, adjustable text sizes, and measurement tables support different access needs. Customizable sound settings let users choose a comfortable pitch range and listening style.

3. What is the intended impact?

Our goal is to help blind and low-vision learners explore Earth science more independently and give educators another way to introduce data.

We hope users will recognize warming trends, compare changes in nighttime lights, and hear seasonal lightning patterns. More broadly, Earthtone demonstrates how designing for accessibility can create useful learning experiences for many people.

4. What tools did you use?

We built Earthtone with HTML, CSS, JavaScript, browser-based audio synthesis, and GitHub Pages. We used the NVDA screen reader and Microsoft Windows Magnifier during development to guide accessibility improvements.

Our data sources include NASA GISTEMP v4 and NASA Scientific Visualization Studio videos showing Black Marble nighttime lights and International Space Station Lightning Imaging Sensor observations.

5. How is your project creative?

Our co-creator’s experience with low vision and her background as a pianist inspired us to treat sound as a way to investigate data.

Earthtone gives users control over how the data sounds. They can preview instruments, choose their lowest and highest notes, and compare continuous pitch mapping with musical scales. A “How the Sound Is Made” section explains the rules, connecting creative exploration with scientific interpretation.

6. What factors did your team consider?

We focused on accessibility, meaningful sound, and scientific transparency. Could users navigate without a mouse? Read controls with a screen reader or magnifier? Understand what a rising note means? Adjust the sound comfortably?

We also considered how audio choices affect interpretation. Musical scales round pitches, and values outside the mapping range reach its limits. Nighttime lights and lightning are video-derived approximations, and lightning observations have limited geographic coverage. We explain these limitations and provide numerical readings alongside the audio.
